meta.title: Who Are You When Nobody Is Approving?
meta.keywords: learning AI tools, peer disapproval, identity, staying small to be liked, curiosity, creative practice

discoverability.social_hook: I got roasted for spending three years gleefully learning AI tools. What actually hurt: realizing how many people only knew how to love me if I stayed small enough to be legible.
discoverability.search_summary: On the cost of staying legible to people whose affection you want. Three years in blissful maker mode learning AI tools, and the contempt that came back — not from strangers, but from people who only knew how to love a smaller version of me. What it took to keep going anyway.

meta.title: AI Is an Art Medium
meta.description: AI is a medium, not a shortcut or threat. Like oil paint, like the camera, like Photoshop — the people exploring it now will make work we can't yet imagine.
meta.keywords: AI as medium, generative AI, art, creative tools, new mediums, technological change in art

discoverability.social_hook: Every generation builds social levees against the rising water of a new medium. The water doesn't care. AI is paint, not a thief — and the people elbow-deep in it now will make work the rest of us can't yet conceive.
discoverability.search_summary: On AI as an artistic medium — like oil paint, the camera, or Photoshop, not a shortcut or a threat. The people working through its rough early years will come out the other side making work we can't conceive of yet. This is not prediction; it's pattern.

meta.title: The Years of Craft Do Not Get a Vote
meta.description: Craft is real, but it doesn't earn you a veto on whether the medium moves. David Byrne didn't copy his sources. He absorbed them, and what came out was him.
meta.keywords: craft, skill, AI tools, expertise, creative practice, generative AI, taste, David Byrne

discoverability.social_hook: I still believe in craft. I still believe in skill. But years of practice don't earn you a veto on whether the medium moves. David Byrne didn't copy his sources — he absorbed them, and what came out was unmistakably him.
discoverability.search_summary: On craft, expertise, and the limits of seniority when the medium changes. Years of refinement give you taste, but they don't grant you a vote on whether new tools are legitimate. The work is to absorb, not to gatekeep.

meta.title: After Scarcity
meta.description: The market isn't being attacked. It's encountering a condition it was never built to survive: abundance. What replaces scarcity logic when the tools change?
meta.keywords: post-scarcity, AI economy, market model, abundance, creative economy, capitalism, future of work

discoverability.social_hook: The market model is dying — not because anyone attacked it, but because it encountered a condition it was never built to survive: abundance. What replaces scarcity logic when the tools change?
discoverability.search_summary: On the economics of the post-AI moment. The market model isn't being murdered; it's encountering abundance, a condition it was never built to handle. The next economy will be built on circulation, contribution, and community — not artificial scarcity.

meta.title: Campfire Logic
meta.description: Before recording, a 'wrong' version of a song barely made sense. A tune was a process, not a product. AI returns us to logic the market professionalized away.
meta.keywords: folk culture, oral tradition, remix culture, AI and authorship, music history, non-market art

discoverability.social_hook: Before recording, a 'wrong' version of a song barely made sense. A tune was a process, not a product. AI is returning us to a logic the market spent a century professionalizing away.
discoverability.search_summary: On non-market logic for art — the folk-process model that predates copyright and persists despite it. Songs were tunes you passed around and changed. AI doesn't break this; it restores it. The question is what kind of community can hold a living-thing model of culture.

meta.title: The Ache in your Heart
meta.description: My mentor said every story needs one ache: a singular gaping wound, explained in too many words. On theme as engine, on writing toward something that hums.
meta.keywords: writing craft, theme, mentorship, story structure, creative writing, the wound, fiction

discoverability.social_hook: My mentor said every story needs one ache — a singular gaping wound, explained in too many words. Theme is the engine. Every conflict has to rhyme with the next. All conflicts point at one truth.
discoverability.search_summary: On theme as the engine of story, and what it means to write toward an ache that hums through every conflict. A meditation on craft mentorship, on staying in the present, and on writing as a way of pointing repeatedly at one human truth.

meta.title: The Preciousness Problem
meta.description: Nobody painted the Mona Lisa alone. Leonardo ran a workshop. Our obsession with singular, precious authorship isn't ancient — it's a market invention, datable.
meta.keywords: authorship, lone genius myth, art history, collaborative art, AI authorship, copyright origins

discoverability.social_hook: Nobody painted the Mona Lisa alone. Leonardo ran a workshop. Our obsession with singular, precious authorship isn't ancient — it's a market invention with a date stamp.
discoverability.search_summary: On the historical invention of the lone-genius author. Workshop collaboration was the norm; singular authorship is a market construct that arrived with copyright and modern publishing. AI doesn't threaten authorship — it threatens the economic fiction we wrapped around it.

meta.title: Rabies Capitalism
meta.description: If you have symptoms of rabies, you're already dead — you just don't know it yet. AI made capitalism so unstable it now fights anything that gets close to it.
meta.keywords: AI and capitalism, post-scarcity, labor, market collapse, generative AI economics, abundance

discoverability.social_hook: If you have symptoms of rabies, you're already dead — you just don't know it yet. AI made capitalism so unstable it now fights anything that gets close to it. This is the lurching.
discoverability.search_summary: On AI as rabies for capitalism — a system thrashing because its core assumption of scarcity just broke. The market model isn't being murdered, it's encountering a condition it was never built to survive. This is the first essay in a series on what comes after.

meta.title: Pull, Not Push: Rebuilding My Presence Backwards
meta.description: I've had more names on the internet than prescription strengths. That era is over. On rebuilding so people come find the work instead of being pushed it.
meta.keywords: personal website, online presence, indie web, RSS, newsletter, writer's platform, pull marketing

discoverability.social_hook: I've had more names on the internet than prescription strengths. That era is over. I'm rebuilding so people come find the work — not get it pushed at them by an algorithm.
discoverability.search_summary: On rebuilding an online presence backwards — a permanent home for the work, RSS and newsletters as the connective tissue, and the deliberate refusal of platform metrics. Pull, not push. A writer's manifesto for the post-feed era.

meta.title: Why the 10% Productivity Plateau Should Worry You
meta.description: AI adoption hit 92.6%. AI-authored code is 26.9% of production. Productivity gains: stuck at 10%. The bottleneck was never the tools. It's everything around them.
meta.keywords: AI productivity, software engineering metrics, developer productivity, AI adoption, GitHub Copilot, code review bottleneck

discoverability.social_hook: AI adoption hit 92.6%. AI-authored code is 26.9% of all production code. Productivity gains: stuck at 10%. The bottleneck was never the tools — it's everything around them.
discoverability.search_summary: On the 10% productivity plateau showing up across every major AI-coding-tools dataset. Adoption is saturated. Output is measurable. Gains have flattened. The bottleneck was never the speed of code generation — it's review, integration, and trust at the seams.

meta.title: Volume Is Not Velocity
meta.description: GitClear analyzed 211M changed lines across major tech repos. Refactoring is dropping, duplication rising. We're writing more code and quietly degrading the thing.
meta.keywords: code quality, AI coding tools, refactoring, code duplication, software metrics, GitClear, technical debt

discoverability.social_hook: GitClear analyzed 211M lines of code across Google, Microsoft, Meta, and enterprise repos. Refactoring is dropping. Duplication is rising. We're writing more code and quietly degrading the thing we're building.
discoverability.search_summary: On the GitClear 211M-line dataset showing AI-era code quality regression. Refactoring fell from 25% to under 10%; duplication rose from 8.3% to 12.3%. Volume is up. The codebase is louder, busier, and worse. Velocity is what we mean — and we are not getting it.

meta.title: The Hidden Tax on Senior Engineers
meta.description: AI didn't reduce demand on your best engineers. It redirected it. After Copilot: 6.5% more code reviewed, 19% less original work. The senior tax is real.
meta.keywords: senior engineers, AI productivity, Copilot impact, code review, engineering management, mentorship tax

discoverability.social_hook: AI didn't reduce demand on your best engineers. It redirected it. After Copilot: senior engineers reviewed 6.5% more code and produced 19% less original work. The tax landed on the people you can least afford to overload.
discoverability.search_summary: On the Xu et al. (2025) finding that AI coding tools redistribute workload toward senior engineers. Peripheral contributors output more; core maintainers shift to review. The tax lands on the people whose original work mattered most. A structural problem, not a temporary one.

meta.title: Carl
meta.description: I'm Carl. I work at Floor-Mart. I always have, always will, forever and ever, amen. A short story about retail, androids, and being designed for a role.
meta.keywords: short fiction, science fiction, AI, retail dystopia, android, labor, character study

discoverability.social_hook: My name is Carl. I work at Floor-Mart. I always have worked at Floor-Mart and I always will work at Floor-Mart, forever and ever, amen. A short story.
discoverability.search_summary: Short fiction. Carl is an android working in a retail parking lot in the middle of winter. Androids don't get cold. They do, however, notice things. A story about labor, design, and the quiet theology of being made for a role you can't leave.

meta.title: Why AI Helps Juniors and Slows Down Seniors
meta.description: Junior developers benefit more from AI than senior ones. Sometimes dramatically more. Sometimes seniors get slower. Not a glitch — the structure of expertise.
meta.keywords: AI productivity, senior developers, junior developers, software engineering, expertise, mental models, code review

discoverability.social_hook: Junior developers benefit more from AI than senior ones. Sometimes dramatically more. Sometimes seniors get slower. This isn't a temporary glitch — it's what happens when you insert a confident, fast, sometimes-wrong assistant into the middle of expertise.
discoverability.search_summary: On the experience gap in AI-assisted coding. Across every major study, juniors gain more than seniors; under certain conditions seniors lose ground. The cause is structural: expertise is exactly the thing AI can disrupt, because expertise IS the calibrated bullshit detector AI hasn't earned.

meta.title: The Photograph of a River
meta.description: Every AI productivity study is a photograph of a river. By the time you develop the film, the water has moved. Read the study, not the headline.
meta.keywords: AI productivity studies, METR study, research methodology, software engineering research, AI adoption, study limitations

discoverability.social_hook: Every AI productivity study is a photograph of a river. By the time you develop the film, the water has moved. METR found AI users took 19% longer. The number was real. It's also already old.
discoverability.search_summary: On reading AI productivity research honestly. The METR study was rigorous and its 19%-slower finding was real for its moment. The tools, the workflows, and the people have all moved since. The research is a snapshot of water — useful, but not the river.

meta.title: I Thought I Had a Bad Memory. I Don't.
meta.description: Sighted people offload remembering to the world: keys by the door, cap ajar on the counter. Take the world away and the brain builds something different.
meta.keywords: blindness, memory, cognition, gist memory, neurodivergence, embodied cognition, white cane chronicles

discoverability.social_hook: I thought I had a bad memory. Turns out sighted people offload most of theirs to the world around them: cap ajar on the counter, keys by the door. Take that away and the brain builds something different. Maybe better.
discoverability.search_summary: On the gist-memory advantage of blind cognition. Sighted memory is heavily scaffolded by environment — visual confirmation of objects standing in for remembering the act. Blind cognition has to do without that scaffold, and what it builds in compensation is not a deficit but a different architecture.
